subject: Cognitive Science
title: Neural Basis of Categories
description: Learn Neural Basis of Categories in one minute.

hook.text: A patient with brain damage can name tools but not animals. Categories live in the brain.

buildup.text: Category-specific deficits show that different types of knowledge occupy different neural regions.

discovery.text: Living things rely on visual features stored near visual cortex. Tools activate motor areas.

twist.text: But it's not a clean map. Recognizing a tiger also activates fear circuits in the amygdala.

climax.text: A concept is a pattern of activation spread across brain regions, not a single filing cabinet.

quiz.question: What do category-specific deficits tell us?
options: Different categories rely on different brain regions
All categories use one brain area

details.summary: Brain imaging reveals that different types of categories activate different neural regions. Living things activate temporal areas related to visual features. Tools activate regions linked to motor function and use. Category-specific deficits after brain damage confirm this distributed organization.
details.whyItMatters: The brain does not store categories in one place but distributes them across feature-relevant regions. This architecture explains why brain damage can selectively impair specific categories.
takeaways: Living things and tools activate different brain regions
Category knowledge is distributed across feature systems
Brain damage can selectively impair specific category knowledge

faq.question: What are category-specific deficits?
faq.answer: Some patients with brain damage lose knowledge of living things like animals while retaining tool knowledge, or vice versa. These dissociations show that category knowledge is organized by the type of features that define the category, not by the category label itself.

faq.question: Where are categories stored in the brain?
faq.answer: Categories are not stored in single locations but are distributed patterns. The anterior temporal lobe acts as a hub integrating features from across the brain. Visual features, motor associations, and functional knowledge are stored in their respective sensory and motor regions.
